title: Add invocation-priority-decayer metric and token-cost oracle for quieter SLOs
author: Nina Patel
description:
Background: We see frequent noisy SLO alerts driven by short-lived token-cost spikes from high-priority invocations (interactive debugging and REPL use). These spikes often cascade into alert churn because the alerting rules treat each invocation window equally and are sensitive to single high-cost tails. This PR introduces an invocation-priority-decayer metric and a derived token-cost-oracle aggregation to 1) downweight ephemeral priority bursts, 2) provide a deterministic per-invocation cost estimate for alerting, and 3) enable quieter SLO rules with reduced false positives.

What this PR does: adds server-side metric instrumentation, dashboard panels, alert rule adjustments, and sampling helpers: - invocation-priority-decayer: a per-invocation exponential decay counter capturing recent priority history (labels: tenant_id, route, priority_tier) - token-cost-oracle: a compact aggregate that fuses measured token-cost, KV-prefetch contribution, and decayed-priority to yield an adjusted cost estimate used in alerts - sampled-contextualizer: sampling hook that tags traces used by the oracle for easy backfill and debugging - dashboards: new dashboard JSON with oracle visualizations and a quiet-window simulator - alert rules: adjusted cost SLO rule that uses oracle_estimate and a 5m quiet-window fallback policy (auto-mute for single-interval spikes)

Checklist: - [x] Instrumentation added and unit-tested - [x] Dashboard JSON validated in staging - [x] Alert rule updated with canary release and documented - [x] Migration notes and runtime config knobs added - [x] Docs (observability/priority-decayer.md) and upgrade guidance included

Migration / runtime knobs: the decayer is controlled via feature flags (obs.priority_decayer.enabled) and decay_rate per-tenant. Default is opt-in in staging for 72 hours then ramp to all. Operators can tune quiet-window length and oracle weight.

Testing notes: initial integration run failed due to missing metric label on some legacy invocations; fixed by commit that adds safe-labeling fallback. Full e2e and canary checked on staging with synthetic high-priority traffic and saw a 62% reduction in alert firing for known noisy tenants with <1% impact on true positive alerts.

Motivation / rationale: rather than moving alert thresholds (which masks regressions), the oracle provides a mechanistic cost estimate that reflects expected steady-state cost while allowing the alerting system to remain responsive to real regressions. This reduces operational toil for SREs and gives product teams a clearer signal when model/unit changes actually affect serving economics.

review_comments: Aaron Cho: Please add an integration test that simulates legacy invocations which lack 'priority_tier' and ensure the safe-labeling fallback is exercised.
Nina Patel: Added f0a1b22 with a unit and integration test that injects legacy headers; the metric now emits priority_tier=unknown for older clients.

Maya Stein: The metric cardinality looks OK in the small canary, but we should cap tenant-level decay_rate to avoid high-cardinality churn. Suggest adding a tenant-level max label bucketing in metricExporter( ).
Nina Patel: Added a guard in invocation_priority_decayer.go to bucket decay_rate into 'low|medium|high' labels before export. Also documented the cardinality implications in the migration notes.
Leo Anders: Approved after verifying dashboards and that CI greened on the rerun. Left a small nits comment about log message verbosity which Nina addressed in the last commit.
release_notes:
- Introduced invocation-priority-decayer metric and token-cost-oracle aggregation to reduce noise in cost SLOs.
- New dashboard panels for oracle visualization and quiet-window simulation.
- Updated cost SLO rule to use oracle_estimate with a canary rollout.
- Migration guide: enable obs.priority_decayer.enabled in staging and monitor cardinality; default is opt-in for 72h.
